title: Sky Atlas
intro: Find the Orion Nebula, read its height above your horizon, or see where your own image fits on the sky.
dataset: Start Citizen Astronomy (CAst). The Orion and Moon exercises use the built-in atlas. For the optional overlay exercise, bring an image with a sky-coordinate solution.
outcome: Find an object by name, plan for a site and time, choose which sky layers to display, and place a registered image on the map.
heroAlt: Sky Atlas centered on Orion, with constellation lines linking bright stars, Rigel and Sirius labeled, and the Milky Way behind the chart.

steps.title: Open Sky Atlas
steps.requires: Start CAst. If you are in another workspace, use **Mode → Choose Mode…** to return to the launcher.
actions: Under **Explore, Visualize & Process**, click the **Sky Atlas** card (1).
steps.check: The sky replaces the launcher. Stars are drawn as points, while circles mark cataloged objects. You can explore immediately, without opening an image folder.
steps.alt: Sky Atlas outlined in the launcher row alongside Sky Explorer and HR Diagram.

steps.title: Reveal the bottom controls
steps.requires: [Open Sky Atlas](#launch).
actions: Move the pointer to the bottom center of the sky and leave it there for a moment. A row of square buttons slides up in the outlined area (1).
Hold the pointer over an icon to read its tooltip. Move back into the sky to let the controls slide away.
steps.check: The first button is a magnifying glass. The bar also contains the clock, observing site, sky layers and settings. If it disappears, move the pointer back to the bottom center of the atlas.
steps.alt: Full chart with the bottom-center dock outlined.

steps.title: Pan across the sky and zoom
steps.requires: [Open the atlas](#launch). Use this whenever you want to explore by eye.
actions: Place the pointer in the marked part of the sky (1). Hold the left mouse button, drag a short distance and release.
Roll the mouse wheel forward to zoom in, or backward to see a wider area. Look at **FOV** along the bottom edge of the map. FOV means field of view.
steps.check: Dragging brings different stars into the frame. A smaller FOV spans fewer degrees of sky and lets you distinguish objects that previously appeared close together.
steps.alt: Sky chart with a small rectangle in the central star field showing where to start the drag.

groups.title: Find a target and read its details

steps.title: Open the sky search
steps.requires: [Reveal the bottom controls](#dock).
actions: Click the magnifying glass at the left end of the bar (1). Its tooltip says **Search the sky**.
steps.check: A search window opens with a box for a name, catalog ID or alias. It can find entries in downloaded catalogs even when their map layers are hidden.
steps.alt: Bottom bar with its leftmost magnifying glass marked.

steps.title: Find the Orion Nebula (M42)
steps.requires: The [search window](#search-open) is open.
actions: Click the search box (1) and type **M42**. Wait for the results to appear.
Click the **Nebula  Orion Nebula** row (2), or press **Enter** while that row is highlighted. Check that its catalog line says **Messier**.
steps.check: The search closes, the chart centers on the Orion Nebula and an information panel appears at upper left. The number of other matches depends on which catalogs are installed.
steps.alt: Search box containing M42 and the Orion Nebula result in the Messier catalog.

steps.title: Read where the object is
steps.requires: [Find M42](#search), or locate a labeled star or object in the atlas.
actions: Click the object’s marker in the sky (1) to pin it. Double-click a visible marker if you also want to center it.
Read the panel at upper left (2). **RA** and **Dec** locate the object on the celestial sphere. **Alt** tells you how far above or below the local horizon it is. **Az** gives its compass direction.
steps.check: At Greenwich on 6 January 2026 at 23:00 UTC, this example places M42 about **33°** above the horizon toward the south. Your Alt and Az depend on your own site and time.
steps.alt: Marker centered on the Orion Nebula and a pinned panel showing its name, magnitude and coordinates.

steps.title: Open a catalog entry or research papers
steps.requires: [Pin a named object](#pin).
actions: In the marked row below the object type (1), click **SIMBAD** for an object record, **ADS** for papers, or **VizieR** for catalog data.
Return to CAst when you want to continue exploring the map.
steps.check: Your browser opens the chosen service with the object identifier. The services need an internet connection. The links available depend on the selected object.
steps.alt: Pinned Orion Nebula panel with the SIMBAD, ADS and VizieR links outlined together.

steps.title: Search for the Moon
steps.requires: [Open sky search](#search-open). Set the [site](#site) and [UTC time](#time) first if you want a view for a particular night.
actions: Type **Moon** in the search box (1).
Select **Natural Satellite  Moon** under **Solar System** (2).
steps.check: The atlas centers on the Moon’s position for the selected site and time and pins its details. At a wide field of view it may appear only as a small disk.
steps.alt: Moon in the search field with the Solar System result highlighted.

links.label: Zoom in on the lunar disk

steps.title: Inspect the lunar disk
steps.requires: [Select the Moon](#moon-search). If the Moon is below your horizon, turn off the [ground layer](#horizon) to inspect it anyway.
actions: Place the pointer over the lunar disk (1) and roll the wheel forward a few notches at a time. If the disk slips toward an edge, drag to bring it back toward the middle.
Roll backward when you want to see the surrounding field again.
steps.check: The lit part of the Moon fills more of the view. Its shape and orientation follow the selected observing time and site.
steps.alt: Close-up of the rendered Moon, with its bright terrain and dark limb enclosed by a numbered outline.

groups.title: Plan for a place and time

steps.title: Open Observer Location
steps.requires: [Reveal the dock](#dock).
actions: Click the map-pin icon (1). Its tooltip says **Observer location**.
steps.check: The Observer Location window opens with a map and a **Saved Site** panel. Its coordinates set the observer position used by CAst.
steps.alt: Bottom-center controls with the location pin outlined.

links.label: Enter a site or reuse one

steps.title: Set your observing site
steps.requires: [Open Observer Location](#site-open). Use your own coordinates or the Greenwich example shown.
actions: In **Name** (1), enter a label. In **Latitude** (2) and **Longitude** (3), enter degrees. South and west use negative values. For this example enter **Greenwich**, **51.48**, and **0.00**.

Enter **Elevation** in metres (4), for example **46**. Leave **Keep this site in quick-switch presets** checked if you want to use it again. For a previously saved site, pick it under **Saved Sites** and click **Load** instead.
Click **Save Location** (5).
steps.check: The window closes and the atlas footer shows the active site. Altitude, azimuth and the horizon now refer to that location.
steps.alt: Saved Site controls showing Greenwich, latitude, longitude, elevation, and Save Location.

steps.title: Freeze the sky and open the clock
steps.requires: [Reveal the dock](#dock).
actions: Look at the third button from the left (1). If its tooltip says **Pause time**, click it. When the clock is paused, the button shows a play triangle, as in the screenshot.
Click the **Date and time** button immediately to its left (2).
steps.check: A UTC date and time editor appears above the dock. Pausing makes it easier to compare two moments while holding the sky still.
steps.alt: Clock pause/play control and the adjacent date-time control numbered in click order.

links.label: Enter a time or advance one hour

steps.title: Choose a UTC date or step one hour
steps.requires: [Open the date and time popup](#time-open).
actions: Click the date and time field (1). Select and edit each part, or open the calendar to pick the date. For the Orion example, set **6 January 2026, 23:00 UTC**.
Click **+1 h** (2) to jump one hour forward. Use **-1 h** to undo that jump. **+1 d** and **-1 d** change the day.

For the Orion example, click outside the popup to keep the selected time. If you want to return to the present, click **Now** (3) before closing the popup. Click the play triangle on the dock when you want time to advance again.
steps.check: The UTC field changes to the selected moment. With a target pinned, compare **Alt** and **Az** before and after the hour jump.
steps.alt: UTC date editor, +1 h and Now buttons marked separately.

links.label: Read the altitude at this time
Find the Moon at this time

steps.title: Choose the kind of grid
steps.requires: [Reveal the dock](#dock).
actions: Click **Toggle equatorial grid** (1) for right ascension and declination lines. Click it again to hide them.
Click **Toggle alt-az grid** (2) for the altitude and azimuth lines at your observing site. For an easy comparison, show one grid at a time.
steps.check: Each button switches its own grid. Use equatorial coordinates to match a catalog position and local coordinates to decide where to look from the ground.
steps.alt: Two adjacent grid buttons numbered on the dock.

steps.title: Compare the two grids on one field
steps.requires: [Find M42](#search) and zoom out enough to see several stars. For the same sky orientation, use the example [site](#site) and [time](#time).
actions: In the atlas, use the marked grid button (1) for the view you want. If the other grid is still visible, click its button to turn it off.
Use **Equatorial** and **Local horizon** above the tutorial screenshot to compare the same frozen sky. Follow a bright star as you switch diagrams.
steps.check: The stars keep their positions in this comparison. The two grids run in different directions because one follows Earth’s rotation axis and the other follows the observer’s horizon.
steps.alt: Equatorial grid drawn across Orion, with the responsible button marked.

comparison.label: Local horizon
comparison.alt: The same chart with altitude and azimuth lines and the corresponding dock button marked.

steps.title: Trace the constellations
steps.requires: [Reveal the dock](#dock).
actions: Click **Toggle constellations** (1), the connected-points icon immediately to the right of the grid buttons.
Look for lines joining the brighter stars. Click the same button again to hide the outlines and names.
steps.check: In the Orion field, the lines help you trace the pattern around the nebula even when other catalogs are crowded.
steps.alt: A wide chart with constellation outlines and the connected-points dock button highlighted.

steps.title: See which objects are above the ground
steps.requires: [Set your site](#site) and [UTC time](#time). Reveal the bottom dock.
actions: Click **Toggle ground and horizon** (1). Drag the map or zoom out until the horizon crosses the frame.
Look above the horizon line for visible sky. If a selected object falls below the line, switch the ground off to inspect it, or try another observing time.
steps.check: The ground covers the part of the celestial sphere below your local horizon. An object above the line has positive altitude.
steps.alt: An all-sky view with the ground across its lower portion and the horizon control outlined.

steps.title: Open the catalog settings
steps.requires: [Reveal the dock](#dock).
actions: Click the gear labeled **Sky Atlas settings** (1), next to the custom overlay button.
steps.check: **Sky Atlas Settings** opens with two pages, **Stars** and **Deep-Sky Objects**.
steps.alt: Dock with the settings gear outlined.

steps.title: Set the faintest stars to draw
steps.requires: [Open Sky Atlas Settings](#settings-open) and click **Stars** in the left column.
actions: Drag **Limiting magnitude** (1). Move right to include fainter stars, left to keep the brighter ones. Read the estimated star count and download size under **Star catalog download** before confirming.
Click **OK** at the bottom of the dialog to apply. If a download starts, keep using the map while it runs. Zoom in to see the fainter stars as they become available.
steps.check: At a modest limit the estimate names Hipparcos. Deeper limits may require larger Tycho-2 or Gaia data downloads. **Cancel** in the settings dialog restores your saved values.
steps.alt: Stars page with the limiting-magnitude slider and Hipparcos download estimate visible.

links.label: Zoom in to inspect the field

steps.title: Choose which deep-sky objects and names appear
steps.requires: [Open Sky Atlas Settings](#settings-open).
actions: Click **Deep-Sky Objects** (1). Under **Catalogs to show**, check **Messier** (2) for the Orion Nebula example. Select any additional catalogs you need.
Drag **Label limiting magnitude** (3) to the right to label fainter objects. The separate **Object limiting magnitude** controls which markers appear.
Click **OK** (4) to apply. Enabling a catalog for the first time may start a download.
steps.check: The map displays the enabled objects within the chosen brightness limits. Zoom in to bring out labels in crowded fields.
steps.alt: Deep-Sky Objects page with its navigation row, Messier checkbox, label limit slider and OK button outlined.

steps.title: Open the display options
steps.requires: [Reveal the dock](#dock).
actions: Click **Sky View options** (1), the sliders icon between the settings gear and the full-screen button.
steps.check: A popup opens with Milky Way and constellation controls and a **Reset View** button at the bottom.
steps.alt: Bottom toolbar with the sliders icon highlighted.

steps.title: Change the Milky Way background
steps.requires: [Open Sky View options](#options-open).
actions: Check **Milky Way** (1) to show the background.
Open **Preset** (2) and try **Dark sky** or **Atlas**. Drag **Opacity** (3) left to make the backdrop less prominent, or right to bring it forward.
Click in the sky to close the popup.
steps.check: The haze and dark lanes behind the stars change in strength. Object positions stay fixed while you adjust the background.
steps.alt: Milky Way group with its on/off checkbox, preset list and opacity slider outlined.

steps.title: Return to the opening view
steps.requires: [Open Sky View options](#options-open) when you have panned or zoomed away from your starting point.
actions: At the bottom of the popup, click **Reset View** (1).
steps.check: The camera moves back toward the opening wide field near Orion. You can search for a target again from here.
steps.alt: Reset View button marked below the constellation style controls.

groups.title: Place your own image on the sky

steps.title: Open the custom image overlays
steps.requires: [Reveal the dock](#dock). Use this branch to display an image of a field you photographed.
actions: Click **Custom sky map overlays** (1), the four-square icon between the horizon button and the settings gear.
steps.check: The **Custom Sky Map** popup opens. A survey is a named collection of your registered images.
steps.alt: Dock with the custom sky map overlay button outlined.

links.label: Display a survey I already have

steps.title: Open the survey editor
steps.requires: [Open Custom Sky Map](#overlay-open).
actions: Click **Edit Surveys** (1).
steps.check: A **Custom Sky Map Surveys** window opens. The left side lists your surveys and the right side lists the images in the selected survey.
steps.alt: Custom Sky Map popup with Edit Surveys marked.

steps.title: Create a survey for one field or filter
steps.requires: [Open the survey editor](#edit-survey).
actions: Click **New Survey** (1) below the list on the left.
steps.check: A new entry appears and its Name, Filter and image controls become available.
steps.alt: Survey editor with New Survey highlighted below the list.

links.label: Name it and add an image

steps.title: Name the survey and add an image
steps.requires: [Create a new survey](#new-survey), or click a survey that you already have. Keep a registered image handy. Registration means the file contains the sky position for its pixels.
actions: Click **Name** (1) and give the collection a recognizable name. The example uses **Lagoon field**. Optionally choose a **Filter** (2), such as **Ha** for a hydrogen-alpha image.
Click **Add Image…** (3).
steps.check: A file picker opens. CAst accepts FITS, XISF, PNG and TIFF overlays.
steps.alt: Name, Filter and Add Image button marked on the survey’s detail panel.

steps.title: Select the registered image
steps.requires: The file picker opened from [Add Image](#add-image). Use a plate-solved file. For a PNG or TIFF, a matching FITS sidecar can supply the sky coordinates.
actions: Browse to the image or enter its name (1). The illustrated example selects **Lagoon.png** and keeps its matching **Lagoon.fits** coordinate file in the same folder.
Click **Open** (2) and wait for the import. If the image lacks a usable coordinate solution, the app attempts a plate solve. A solved FITS or XISF image is the simplest starting point.
steps.check: The file name appears in the survey’s Images list after import succeeds.
steps.alt: The file name field containing Lagoon.png and the Open button marked in order.

steps.title: Check the imported image and save
steps.requires: [Import an image](#choose-image) and wait for its name to appear.
actions: Check the **Images** list (1) under the correct survey name. To add another exposure or tile, repeat **Add Image…**.
Click **OK** (2) to save the collection and return to the atlas.
steps.check: Your named collection is available in the Survey list. Its images are drawn at the coordinates supplied by each image’s sky solution.
steps.alt: Survey editor with Lagoon.png in the images list and OK outlined.

steps.title: Show an existing survey and set its opacity
steps.requires: [Open Custom Sky Map](#overlay-open). At least one survey must contain an [imported image](#choose-image).
actions: Open **Survey** (1) and choose your collection. The example uses **Lagoon field (Ha)**. Check **Show custom sky overlays** (2) to display it.
Drag **Opacity** (3) left to blend the image into the atlas, or right to make it stronger. Click away from the popup when you have finished.
[Search](#search-open) for the target in your image and zoom in. Choosing a survey keeps your current view, so you may need to travel to its field.
steps.check: The image appears in its sky footprint. If you cannot see a difference, confirm the right survey is selected, its checkbox is on, and the map is centered on its target.
steps.alt: Survey dropdown, Show custom sky overlays checkbox and opacity slider numbered on the popup.

links.label: Compare the registered image with the atlas

steps.title: Compare the overlay with the atlas alone
steps.requires: [Display your survey](#show-survey) and zoom toward its target. The example uses the Lagoon Nebula, **M8**.
actions: Find the marked field (1). Use **Atlas only** and **With image** above the tutorial screenshot to inspect the change at fixed scale.
To repeat it in CAst, toggle **Show custom sky overlays** in [Custom Sky Map](#show-survey) while keeping the view on the same sky position.
steps.check: The Lagoon Nebula and nearby catalog markers stay in the same positions. The registered image adds fine structure and many faint stars inside the footprint.
steps.alt: Atlas view centered on the Lagoon Nebula with the target area marked before the image is shown.

comparison.label: With image
comparison.alt: Same position and scale with Lagoon.png visible over the marked area.
